title: Anonymous forum discourse quality studies
description: Empirical research on online platforms (e.g., 4chan vs. persistent-identity forums) consistently shows that anonymous or ephemeral-identity spaces exhibit higher rates of argument repetition, lower rates of concession, and reduced convergence on shared conclusions. Kilner & Hoadley (2005) and later studies on Reddit pseudonymity vs. full anonymity corroborate the pattern.
source: Comparative studies of discourse quality across anonymous vs. pseudonymous online platforms (meta-review)

title: Walton's commitment-store model of dialogue
description: Douglas Walton's formal dialogue theory posits that productive argumentation requires a 'commitment store' — a running record of propositions each participant has asserted or conceded. Persistent identity is the natural binding key for commitment stores; without it, the store cannot be attributed and commitments become unenforceable, collapsing the dialogue structure.
source: Walton, D. (1984). Logical Dialogue-Games and Fallacies; Walton & Krabbe (1995) Commitment in Dialogue

title: Reputation systems and epistemic improvement
description: Platforms with persistent reputation systems (Stack Exchange, academic citation networks) show measurably higher rates of error correction and knowledge convergence than platforms without. Reputation acts as a proxy for accumulated dialectical track record, incentivizing participants to maintain consistency and respond to defeaters rather than abandon and restart positions.
source: Studies on Stack Exchange quality metrics; Mamykina et al. (2011) Design lessons from Stack Overflow; citation network analyses

title: Historical example: Scientific societies and persistent membership
description: The epistemic productivity of early scientific societies (Royal Society, Académie des Sciences) depended heavily on persistent membership where individuals' prior claims could be recalled and challenged. Disputes like Newton-Leibniz or the oxygen theory controversy progressed precisely because participants' identities persisted, allowing arguments to accumulate and defeaters to stick across years of correspondence.
source: Shapin & Schaffer (1985) Leviathan and the Air-Pump; historical accounts of Royal Society proceedings
